title: Banking job cuts collide with a specialist regulatory talent shortage
full_text:
Australian banks cut about 8,000 roles in 2025, yet compliance and transformation specialists remain scarce and expensive to secure
Australia's largest banks, insurers and super funds cut roughly 8,000 permanent jobs across 2025 in a bid to save money.
At the same time, many of those same organisations are struggling to find the specialist people they need to meet a string of new government rules landing one after another, according to data from Outsized.
Regulators have set a run of deadlines requiring banks, insurers and super funds to prove they can withstand major disruptions, catch money laundering and other financial crime, be held accountable when things go wrong, and disclose their climate-related risks.
Meeting these deadlines requires people with a rare mix of technical and regulatory know-how, and there simply aren't enough of them to go around.
Former regulators and senior executives brought in on short-term contracts to advise on this work are now charging up to $4,000 a day, while qualified actuaries and specialists who manage super fund mergers are similarly hard to find.
Two workforce conversations pulling in different directions
Martin Bouroncle, client partner and commercial director for ANZ at Outsized, told HRD the mismatch comes down to cost-cutting and workforce planning happening as separate conversations inside the same organisation.
"It's a perfect storm,” Bouroncle said. "There's the conversation around the need to watch expense lines. But then at the same time, you've got workforce planning evolution with the prominence of AI and efficiencies."
He said the two conversations are not always properly connected. "It does seem like one conversation is having material impact on the other and vice versa. So it's about how do we bring those together."
Bouroncle pointed to reporting on AI adoption reshaping skills and governance priorities for HR as evidence the strategic questions have shifted.
"Back in the day used to be how do we forecast the number of FTE we might need, whereas these days it's more around what tasks need to be filled in the future and do we need to build capability, buy capability, borrow capability or bot capability?"
Regulatory deadlines are outrunning permanent hiring
Bouroncle said the mismatch is sharpest in financial services because the roles being cut tend to be everyday technology and operations jobs, while the gaps opening up are in specialist positions tied to new regulation.
"We are releasing people, but the paradox is, but we also need people, they're just from different buckets," he said, noting several major reforms are all landing on organisations at once.
"We just don't have that luxury in financial services anymore," he said. "It's about delivering to timelines. So there's a time boundary – initiatives that just have to keep moving."
Sara Kahlau, ANZ lead and global chief people officer at Outsized, framed the shift as a change in what limits transformation.
"For the first time in a generation, capability in Australian financial services is harder to access than capital," Kahlau said.
"The question keeping senior leaders awake has changed; it is no longer can we afford this transformation, but whether we mobilise the people to deliver it before the regulator runs out of patience."
Boards are starting to treat capability as a risk
Bouroncle said the specialist shortage has moved beyond an operational hiring problem and into board-level risk territory, alongside broader strategic workforce planning conversations reshaping how HR teams model capability.
"It's the compliance, it's the regulatory, it's the governance roles ... those capabilities are now starting to bleed into the board-level conversations, where this is now a risk at a board level," he said. "It's out of the operational and it's more of a board-level risk conversation now."
According to Outsized's data, Australian engagements now average 8.5 months with a 57 per cent contract-extension rate, and 68 per cent of independents on the platform have more than ten years' experience.
Kahlau said this reflects a structural change in how institutions use specialist talent. "Specialists are being integrated as operating infrastructure, not contingent labour," she said.
"Five years ago, an independent talent hire was a stopgap brought in to cover a vacancy. Today, they are a deliberate part of how an institution delivers its regulatory programs ... The boundary between the two is now something boards design on purpose, rather than improvise role by role under pressure."
Building a pipeline before the next deadline lands
Bouroncle's advice for HR leaders, relevant to employers already reassessing their 2026 hiring and recruitment plans, is to identify critical programs now and pre-approve roles so a single departure does not stall delivery.
"If you don't have a mobilisation program that can be executed within a week, then you need to think about what needs to change," he said, adding that pairing experienced contractors with junior staff can transfer capability internally over time, though he cautioned this is "not your short-term solution."
He also pointed to a broader shift in worker preference. "A portfolio career is more appealing than it used to be," he said. "The rates are there for those roles that are in demand at any period of time – the rates are there to validate those choices from independents."
